items.title: National Income Aggregates — GDP, GNP, NNP, NDP, NI
items.body:
## What National Income measures

**National Income (NI)** is the total money value of all **final goods and services** produced in an economy in a year. It is the headline gauge of economic performance, living standards and growth.

## The core aggregates

| Aggregate | Meaning | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **GDP** | Value produced **within a country's borders** (by residents + foreigners) | Σ value added by all sectors |
| **GNP** | Value produced by a country's **residents/nationals** anywhere | **GDP + NFIA** |
| **NDP** | GDP net of capital consumption | **GDP − Depreciation** |
| **NNP** | GNP net of capital consumption | **GNP − Depreciation** |
| **NI** | Income accruing to factors of production | **NNP at Factor Cost** |

## The two adjustment axes

- **Domestic ↔ National:** add **Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)** = income earned by residents abroad − income earned by foreigners at home. GDP + NFIA = GNP.
- **Gross ↔ Net:** subtract **Depreciation** (consumption of fixed capital) to move from Gross to Net.
- **Market Price ↔ Factor Cost:** **Factor Cost = Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies**. Market price is what buyers pay; factor cost is what producers actually earn.

## Derived personal aggregates

- **Personal Income (PI):** income actually received by households (incl. transfers).
- **Disposable Income (DI):** PI − direct/personal taxes = what households can spend or save.
keyPoints: GDP = output within a country's borders (residents + foreigners); GNP = output by a country's residents anywhere = GDP + NFIA.
NDP = GDP − Depreciation; NNP = GNP − Depreciation.
National Income (NI) = NNP at Factor Cost.
Factor Cost = Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.
Disposable Income = Personal Income − direct taxes.
items.mnemonic: Two knobs: add NFIA to go Domestic→National; subtract Depreciation to go Gross→Net.

items.title: Nominal vs Real GDP & the GDP Deflator
items.body:
## Two ways to value output

- **Nominal (money) GDP:** valued at **current-year market prices** — rises with both output *and* inflation, so it overstates real growth.
- **Real GDP:** valued at **constant base-year prices** — strips out price change to show the **true change in quantity of goods and services**.

## The GDP deflator

The **GDP deflator** is the broadest price index, capturing every good and service that enters GDP:

$$\text{GDP Deflator} = \frac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{\text{Real GDP}} \times 100$$

- A deflator above 100 means prices have risen since the base year.
- Unlike CPI/WPI (fixed baskets), the deflator covers the **whole economy** and re-weights automatically.

## Why it matters

Real GDP (and its growth rate) is the figure quoted for "economic growth." Comparisons across years must use **real**, not nominal, values.
keyPoints: Nominal GDP uses current prices; Real GDP uses constant base-year prices.
GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100.
The deflator is the most comprehensive price index — covers all goods/services in GDP, unlike fixed-basket CPI/WPI.
Real GDP growth is the true measure of economic growth.
items.mnemonic: Deflator = Nominal over Real ×100 — 'how much of nominal is just prices'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Economics: National Income (Nominal vs Real GDP)

items.title: Three Methods of Calculating National Income
items.body:
## Same total, three viewpoints

Output, income and expenditure are three faces of the **circular flow**, so all three methods yield the **same** national income when measured correctly.

### 1. Product / Value-Added Method (output side)
- Split the economy into **primary, secondary, tertiary** sectors.
- For each sector: **Net Value Added = Gross Value of Output − Intermediate Consumption**.
- Summing net value added gives **GDP at Factor Cost**, avoiding **double counting** (only value added / final goods count).
- *Example:* crops worth ₹1,000 using ₹300 of seeds & fertiliser → value added = **₹700**.

### 2. Income Method (income side)
- Add all **factor incomes** from production: **Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Mixed Income**.
- **Transfer payments** (pensions, scholarships) are **excluded** — they are not earned in production.

### 3. Expenditure Method (spending side)
- **GDP (market price) = C + I + G + (X − M)** — private consumption, investment (gross capital formation, incl. inventories), government spending, and net exports.
- Closed economy with no government: the identity reduces to **I = S** (investment equals savings).
- A **closed economy** has no foreign trade (X = M = 0) and no NFIA, so **GDP = GNP**; an **open economy** trades with the rest of the world.
- **Net exports (X − M)** include **invisibles** — services such as tourism, software and shipping. Spending by **foreign tourists in India is an export** of services (a credit in the accounts).

## Common traps
- Double counting intermediate goods (use value added / final goods only).
- Including transfer payments in the income method.
- Forgetting to subtract imports (M) in the expenditure method.
keyPoints: Product method: GDP at FC = Σ(Gross Value of Output − Intermediate Consumption).
Income method: NI = Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Mixed Income; transfer payments excluded.
Expenditure method: GDP at MP = C + I + G + (X − M).
All three methods give the same figure; only final goods/value added counted to avoid double counting.
Closed economy without government: Investment = Savings (I = S).
Closed economy: no foreign trade, X = M = 0, GDP = GNP; foreign tourists' spending in India = export of services (invisibles).
items.mnemonic: Expenditure GDP = 'C I G NX' — Consumption, Investment, Government, Net eXports.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Economics: Methods of Calculating National Income

items.title: Gross Value Added (GVA) and its link to GDP
items.body:
## What GVA is

**Gross Value Added (GVA)** is the value of output **minus** the value of intermediate inputs — the net contribution of a sector, industry or the whole economy to production. It is measured at **basic prices**.

## GVA ↔ GDP relationship

$$\text{GDP (market price)} = \text{GVA (basic prices)} + \text{Product Taxes} - \text{Product Subsidies}$$

- **GVA** reflects producers' / supply-side performance; **GDP** reflects demand-side value at market prices.
- Since the **2015 revision (base 2011-12)**, India began headlining **GVA at basic prices** alongside GDP, and sectoral analysis is done in GVA terms.

## Why economists watch GVA

- Removes the distortion of changing tax/subsidy rates, giving a cleaner read of **real productive activity** by sector (agriculture, industry, services).
- A gap between GVA growth and GDP growth signals shifting net indirect taxes (e.g. a subsidy cut lifts GDP above GVA).
keyPoints: GVA = Output − Intermediate Consumption; measured at basic prices.
GDP at market price = GVA at basic prices + Product Taxes − Product Subsidies.
GVA is the supply/producer-side measure; GDP is the demand-side, market-price measure.
India began publishing GVA prominently with the 2015 (base 2011-12) national-accounts revision.
Sectoral growth (agri/industry/services) is analysed in GVA terms.
items.mnemonic: GDP = GVA + (product taxes − subsidies): market price sits above basic price by net product taxes.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Economics: National Income; MoSPI National Accounts (GVA at basic prices)

items.title: Base Year, the 2022-23 New Series & Statistical Agencies
items.body:
## Base year of national accounts

A **base year** is the reference year whose constant prices are used to compute **real** GDP; it is periodically revised to reflect the changing structure of the economy.

- **Earlier base year: 2011-12** (adopted in the **January 2015** revision, which also brought GVA at basic prices to the fore).
- **Current base year: 2022-23 (new series released 27 February 2026).** MoSPI's **National Statistical Office (NSO)** revised the base to **2022-23**, guided by the **Advisory Committee on National Accounts Statistics (ACNAS)** chaired by **Prof. Biswanath Goldar**; the new series uses newer data sources such as **GST, MCA-21 corporate filings and PLFS**. The Second Advance Estimates released with it put FY2025-26 real GDP growth at **7.6%**.

## Who compiles the data

- **MoSPI** (Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation) is the nodal ministry; the **NSO** (formed 2019 by merging the **CSO** and **NSSO**) prepares national accounts and releases GDP estimates.
- The **National Statistical Commission (NSC)**, set up in **2005** on the **Rangarajan Commission**'s recommendation, is the apex advisory body for official statistics.

## Historical firsts & difficulties

- **First estimate of India's national income: Dadabhai Naoroji** (in *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India*, 1867-68).
- **First scientific estimate: V.K.R.V. Rao** (1931).
- **National Income Committee (1949)** — the first official post-independence body to estimate national income, chaired by **P.C. Mahalanobis** (members V.K.R.V. Rao and D.R. Gadgil); its work led to the setting up of the **CSO in 1951**.
- **Estimation difficulties:** a large **informal/unorganised sector**, **non-monetised** transactions (barter, self-consumption), the black economy, and poor data on small producers.
keyPoints: Current base year = 2022-23 (new series released 27 Feb 2026); replaced 2011-12 (adopted Jan 2015).
2022-23 new GDP series (released 27 Feb 2026) guided by ACNAS (chaired by Biswanath Goldar), NSO-MoSPI; uses GST, MCA-21, PLFS.
NSO (CSO + NSSO merged in 2019) under MoSPI compiles national accounts; NSC (2005, Rangarajan) is apex advisory body.
First national-income estimate: Dadabhai Naoroji (1867-68); first scientific estimate: V.K.R.V. Rao (1931).
National Income Committee (1949) chaired by P.C. Mahalanobis was the first official post-independence NI body; led to CSO (1951).
Estimation is hard due to the informal sector, non-monetised/self-consumption output and the black economy.
items.mnemonic: Base-year jump: 2011-12 → 2022-23 (new series released Feb 2026); Naoroji first, V.K.R.V. Rao scientific-first.
items.source: MoSPI / PIB — New GDP series with base year 2022-23 (27 Feb 2026); APPSC GK PDF — National Income

items.title: Market Price ↔ Factor Cost & Key Conversion Formulae
items.body:
## The two conversions you must memorise

**1. Market Price ↔ Factor Cost** (net indirect taxes = indirect taxes − subsidies):

$$\text{Factor Cost} = \text{Market Price} - \text{Indirect Taxes} + \text{Subsidies}$$

Market price includes taxes like GST paid by buyers; factor cost strips them out to show true income to factors of production.

**2. Gross ↔ Net** (subtract depreciation) and **Domestic ↔ National** (add NFIA).

## Formula ladder

| Step | Formula |
|---|---|
| GDP at Factor Cost | Σ Value Added by all sectors |
| GNP | GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA) |
| NNP | GNP − Depreciation |
| **National Income** | **NNP at Factor Cost = NNP at Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies** |

## Worked micro-example

Given GDP(MP) = ₹100, NFIA = +₹5, Depreciation = ₹8, Indirect Taxes = ₹10, Subsidies = ₹3:
- GNP(MP) = 100 + 5 = **₹105**
- NNP(MP) = 105 − 8 = **₹97**
- NNP(FC) = **National Income** = 97 − 10 + 3 = **₹90**

## Common trap
A **positive NFIA** makes GNP > GDP; a **negative NFIA** (India's usual case, as outflows to foreign investors exceed Indian earnings abroad) makes **GNP < GDP**.
keyPoints: Factor Cost = Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.
GNP = GDP + NFIA; NNP = GNP − Depreciation.
National Income = NNP at Factor Cost = NNP(MP) − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.
Positive NFIA ⇒ GNP > GDP; India's NFIA is usually negative ⇒ GNP < GDP.
Worked case: GDP(MP) 100, NFIA +5, Dep 8, IT 10, Sub 3 ⇒ NI = 90.
items.mnemonic: MP→FC: 'minus taxes, plus subsidies' (taxes inflate market price, subsidies deflate it).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Methods of Calculating National Income (Important Formulae)

items.title: For Mains — National Income
items.body:
National income is a Paper-IV (Economy & Development) staple: examiners rarely ask "define GDP" and instead probe measurement, reliability and whether GDP captures *development*. Organise the answer around the dimensions below.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| **Concept & aggregates** | GDP → GNP (+NFIA) → NNP (−depreciation) → NI (NNP at factor cost); GVA at basic prices as the supply-side headline |
| **Measurement** | Product/value-added, income, expenditure methods converge on one figure (circular flow) |
| **Data reliability** | Informal sector (~45% of GVA), non-monetised output, black economy, base-year lags; IMF's 2025 low data-grade for India |
| **GDP vs welfare** | Ignores distribution, environment, unpaid work; need HDI, MPI, Gini, green accounting |
| **Reform / way forward** | New **2022-23 base-year series (27 Feb 2026)**; GST/MCA-21/PLFS integration; green & natural-capital accounting |

**Data points & authorities to quote:** new GDP series with base year **2022-23 released 27 Feb 2026** (replacing 2011-12), FY2025-26 real growth ~**7.6%**, GDP ~**₹322.6 lakh crore**; nominal GDP ~**$4.1 trillion** (3rd by PPP); services ~**54%**, industry ~**28%**, agriculture ~**18%** of GVA; **ACNAS (Prof. Biswanath Goldar)** guided the revision; **Dadabhai Naoroji (1867-68)** and **V.K.R.V. Rao (1931)** on the history; **National Income Committee 1949 (Mahalanobis)**; the Nobel-linked **Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi** critique of GDP-as-welfare.

**AP angle:** AP's **GSDP** rests on a large agrarian/fisheries and heavily informal base, so state-income estimation faces acute non-monetised-output and informal-sector gaps; AP is among states that have moved to the 2011-12 (and now 2022-23) GSVA framework and reports fast tertiary-sector growth around its services and construction activity.

**Use in answers:** (1) open by distinguishing *measuring output* from *measuring development*; (2) use a one-line **GDP → NI ladder diagram** to show command over concepts; (3) quote the **2022-23 base-year reform** as the "way forward" that modernises data sources; (4) close with the Stiglitz-Sen line that "what we measure shapes what we strive for" to argue for HDI/MPI/green-GDP supplements.
keyPoints: Frame answers as measurement + reliability + GDP-vs-welfare, not mere definitions.
New base-year series 2022-23 (released 27 Feb 2026) using GST/MCA-21/PLFS is the key 'way forward' point.
GDP ignores distribution, environment and unpaid work — cite HDI, MPI, Gini, green accounting.
Quote FY2025-26 real growth ~7.6%, GDP ~₹322.6 lakh crore, services ~54% of GVA.
AP angle: large informal/agrarian base makes GSDP estimation harder.
items.source: MoSPI/PIB — New GDP series base year 2022-23 (27 Feb 2026); Economic Survey 2025-26; Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Report (2009)
